vignette:
Mrs. A. is an 80-year-old widow who came to therapy at the urging of her daughter. She sits upright in the chair, hands folded in her lap, her silver hair neatly pinned. She speaks with a measured calm, but her eyes are restless, scanning the room as if expecting something to emerge from the corners.

She was born in a small city in the Middle East, the eldest daughter of a schoolteacher and a merchant. She married young, moved to the United States with her husband in the 1960s, and built a career as a social worker. For forty years she worked in a community clinic, helping immigrant families navigate trauma, poverty, and illness. She was known for her quiet persistence, her ability to sit with suffering without flinching. But there is one story she never told her clients.

When her son was five years old, he was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She remembers the day not as a single moment but as a slow, splintering crack in the world. The pediatric oncologist used words like "survival rate" and "protocol." She nodded, took notes, asked the right questions-the social worker inside her took over. She scheduled appointments, arranged childcare for her younger daughter, called insurance companies. Her husband, a construction foreman, could not take time off, so she did it all. She sat in waiting rooms for hours, the fluorescent lights humming, the smell of antiseptic coating her throat. She watched her son's body shrink, his hair fall out in clumps on the pillow. She held his hand during lumbar punctures and learned to see the veins in his arms as a map of fragile hope.

The treatment lasted three years. He survived. He is now a healthy man in his fifties, with children of his own. Mrs. A. should feel relief. She says she does. But her body did not get the memo.

She describes the present as a series of small, sharp intrusions. Every time she hears a child cry in a grocery store, her chest tightens. She cannot watch medical dramas on television-the beeping of a heart monitor sends her back to the pediatric ICU, the way the machines seemed to breathe for her son. She avoids the hospital where he was treated, even though it is now the best in the city. When her granddaughter had a routine vaccination last year, Mrs. A. sat in the car, hands gripping the steering wheel, unable to go inside. She felt a hot, irrational anger at the pediatrician-a woman she had never met-as if the doctor might somehow fail again, even though there was no failure then.

At night, she dreams of hospital corridors that stretch infinitely, of doors that lock behind her. She wakes sweating, heart racing, and lies still until her husband's absence reminds her that he died six years ago. In the morning she makes tea, walks to the window, and tells herself to move on. But the memories have become heavier with age. She no longer works, and the structure that once held her steady is gone. She volunteers twice a week at a senior center, but she finds herself avoiding any conversation about children or illness. If a friend mentions a grandchild with a fever, she changes the subject.

She tells me she is tired of being haunted. She says she has helped hundreds of people heal, and yet she cannot heal herself. Her voice is steady, but her hands tremble slightly when she describes her son's first chemotherapy session-the way he looked up at her and said, "Mama, I'm cold." She looks at her own hands now, the thin skin mapped with veins, and says, "I thought I had put that away. But it never went anywhere. It just waited."
